opus-5.5.text:
I think the forum mattered because it was where I first learned that research is really about communication, not just about solving problems by yourself.

In the ACM class, a lot of us came in with a competitive programming mindset. You get a problem, you solve it, you get the green "accepted," and you move on. That's a good foundation, but it's quite a closed world. The student forum was different. Every week someone had to stand up and present something: a paper they had read, a project they were working on, sometimes just an idea that wasn't fully formed yet. And the rest of us would ask questions, sometimes very naive questions, sometimes very sharp ones.

That experience trained a few things. First, you learned to read papers seriously, because you knew you might have to explain them to your classmates, and they would notice if you didn't really understand. Second, you learned how to tell a story about your work: why does this problem matter, what's the key insight, what's still missing. Later, when I went to grad school and started writing papers and giving talks, I realized that a lot of that intuition came from those early forum sessions.

And I think the third thing, maybe the most important, is that it created a culture where students learned from each other. The teachers were great, but a lot of the energy came from peers. You'd see someone your age present something really exciting, and you'd think, "I want to do something like that too." That kind of peer motivation is very hard to create artificially, and the forum was one of the places where it naturally happened.

So when I look back, it wasn't any single talk that made the difference. It was the habit it built: keep exploring, share what you find, and be open to being questioned. That's pretty much what research is.

r001.rationale: The response says the forum taught him to present and communicate research, but it does not clearly say it developed his confidence to express himself publicly.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the Student Forum was where I first learned what research actually is, before I ever wrote a paper. The ACM class itself was intense, lots of algorithms and competitive programming, but the forum was different. Every week a student would stand up and present something they had been reading or working on, and the rest of us would push back. Nobody held back because you were a classmate.

What that did for me was two things. First, it forced me to read papers early and really understand them, because I knew I would have to explain the idea to people who would ask hard questions. You cannot hide behind vague language when your friends are in the room. Second, it taught me that ideas get better through conversation. I would come in thinking I understood something, and someone would ask a question from a completely different angle, and suddenly I realized I had missed the point.

I think a lot of my later work, XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, came from that habit. Those projects were about building things with other people, taking feedback, iterating, being willing to be wrong in public. That is exactly what the forum trained. It was also just a community. We were a small group that stayed together, argued together, and many of us ended up in research because we had already tasted what it felt like.

So when I say it was important to my training, I mean it shaped how I think, not just what I know. The courses gave me the tools. The forum gave me the mindset.

r001.rationale: The response says the forum required him to present ideas, answer hard questions, and become willing to be wrong in public. It does not clearly credit the forum with developing his confidence to express himself publicly.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important part was learning from one another. In a classroom, you’re often trying to understand something that a teacher already knows how to explain. In a student forum, you have to take more responsibility: figure out what’s interesting, understand it yourself, and then explain it clearly enough that your classmates can discuss it with you.

That process is very valuable training for research. When you present an idea, the questions people ask can reveal gaps in your understanding. And when you listen to someone else, you get exposed to ways of thinking that you might not have discovered on your own. For me, that kind of peer learning—being curious together and being willing to ask questions—is what makes the forum important.

r001.rationale: The response describes peer learning, explaining ideas, and discussing questions, but does not say the forum developed Tianqi Chen’s confidence to express himself publicly.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the most important part was learning from other students. In the Student Forum, we could share what we were exploring, ask questions, and learn about ideas beyond our coursework. Presenting something also pushes you to understand it more deeply—you have to explain why it matters and respond to questions. That experience helped me become more comfortable exploring unfamiliar problems and learning collaboratively, which is an important part of doing research.
